clinicalPearls: The molecular designation for the distal arthrogryposis phenotype clinically recognised as Sheldon-Hall syndrome, sitting between the classic DA1 and severe Freeman-Sheldon DA2A
Features predominantly distal contractures with camptodactyly, ulnar deviation, overlapping fingers and talipes equinovarus
Facial signs are mild: downslanting palpebral fissures, a triangular face and a small mouth without severe microstomia
Caused by variants in the fast-twitch sarcomeric genes TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2 and MYH3, usually autosomal dominant
Nomenclature is being refined so DA2B is often subclassified (for example DA2B3) according to the causative gene
Intellect is normal and there is no progressive muscle weakness
Management follows distal arthrogryposis principles of stretching, serial casting, splinting and selective surgical release
reference.pathophysiology: Distal arthrogryposis type 2B arises from dominant variants in the fast skeletal muscle troponin-tropomyosin-myosin complex (TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3). These variants perturb the calcium-regulated actin-myosin interaction, altering muscle tone during foetal development. Diminished and unbalanced foetal movement permits periarticular fibrosis and fixed distal joint contractures. Because it shares causative genes with Freeman-Sheldon syndrome and with distal arthrogryposis type 1, DA2B represents an intermediate point on a continuous phenotypic and genetic spectrum, corresponding clinically to Sheldon-Hall syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Dysmorphology and limb examination to place the phenotype on the distal arthrogryposis spectrum
Molecular genetic testing (TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3 panel) with subclassification by gene
Three-generation pedigree and examination of relatives for subtle features
Radiographs of hands, feet and spine
Prenatal ultrasound for foetal akinesia in at-risk pregnancies
Feeding and airway assessment where a small mouth is present
redFlags: Feeding or airway difficulty from micrognathia or a small mouth
Features drifting toward the severe Freeman-Sheldon end of the spectrum
Progressive weakness suggesting an alternative myopathy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is favourable, with normal intellect and lifespan; the contractures are static and respond well to physiotherapy and orthopaedic surgery, although some residual limb deformity may persist.
pitfalls: Confusing overlapping nomenclature (DA2B versus Sheldon-Hall) and creating diagnostic uncertainty
Overestimating severity by conflating DA2B with Freeman-Sheldon (DA2A)
Missing a mildly affected parent and misjudging recurrence risk
Delaying stretching and splinting so contractures fixate
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Begin early physiotherapy, serial casting, and splinting for the distal contractures
Reserve orthopaedic surgical release for fixed hand and foot deformities, with Ponseti management of talipes equinovarus
Provide occupational therapy to optimise hand function
Assess and support feeding and the airway where a small mouth limits intake
Follow up recognising normal intellect and lifespan without progressive muscle weakness
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with family examination and gene-based subclassification
